concept.title: TCP vs UDP trade-offs
concept.description: TCP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery via handshakes and retransmissions; UDP sends independent datagrams with lower overhead and latency.
assessmentCriteria: Explains why real-time media often prefers UDP over TCP

promptMarkdown: Why do live video calls usually use UDP instead of TCP, even though UDP can drop packets?

rubric.criterion: Explains that TCP retransmits lost packets and enforces in-order delivery, which introduces delay (head-of-line blocking)
Explains that for live video, a slightly late frame is useless, so skipping a dropped packet keeps latency low

idealAnswer: TCP guarantees ordered delivery by pausing and retransmitting any lost packet. In a live call, waiting to resend a video frame from half a second ago stalls everything behind it and creates noticeable lag; it is better to drop the missing frame and stay live, which UDP allows with lower overhead.

answers.text: TCP stops to resend dropped packets so everything arrives in order, which creates lag in a live call. With video you'd rather glitch for one frame and keep going in real time than freeze while waiting for old data, so UDP's fire-and-forget approach keeps latency low.
TCP retransmissions + ordering stall live frames. Late video is useless, so UDP drops losses instead of lagging.
Because UDP is faster and has less overhead than TCP, which is good for video calls.
UDP compresses video frames automatically so they fit through a smaller internet connection, whereas TCP only handles text.

concept.title: Why bond prices fall when interest rates rise
concept.description: Existing fixed-coupon bonds become less attractive when newly issued bonds pay higher rates, so their market price drops until yields match.
assessmentCriteria: Explains the inverse relationship between interest rates and existing bond prices

promptMarkdown: You hold a 10-year bond paying a fixed 3% coupon. Suddenly market interest rates for similar new bonds jump to 5%. What happens to the market price of your bond, and why?

rubric.criterion: States that the market price of the existing bond falls
Explains that buyers can now get 5% on new bonds, so they will only buy the 3% bond at a discount that raises its effective yield toward 5%

idealAnswer: Its market price falls. Because investors can now buy new bonds paying 5%, nobody will pay full face value for a bond locked at 3%. The price drops to a discount so that the lower coupon plus the gain at maturity gives a buyer roughly a 5% yield.

answers.text: The price drops. Why would anyone pay full price for my 3% bond when brand-new ones pay 5%? I have to sell it at a discount so the buyer's total return matches the new 5% market rate.
The price goes down because interest rates and bond prices move in opposite directions.
The price rises because higher interest rates mean bonds in general are paying more money.

concept.title: What gluten does in bread dough
concept.description: Hydrated wheat proteins form an elastic network that traps fermentation gas bubbles so dough rises and holds structure.
assessmentCriteria: Explains that gluten forms an elastic mesh that traps gas produced by yeast

promptMarkdown: What role does the gluten network play when bread dough rises?

rubric.criterion: Describes gluten as a stretchy/elastic protein network in the dough
Explains that it traps the CO2 gas bubbles made by yeast so the dough expands instead of letting the gas escape

idealAnswer: Gluten forms an elastic mesh of linked proteins throughout the dough. As yeast ferments sugars and releases carbon dioxide, that stretchy network traps the gas in tiny pockets so the dough inflates and keeps its shape when baked.

answers.text: Gluten is a stretchy web of proteins that catches the carbon dioxide bubbles the yeast makes. Because it stretches without tearing right away, the trapped gas inflates the dough instead of leaking out.
Gluten gives bread its chewy texture and holds the dough together.
Gluten reacts with warm water to produce carbon dioxide gas, which makes the bread rise.

concept.title: Why you shouldn't rebase a shared public branch
concept.description: Rebasing creates new commit hashes for replayed commits, causing diverged histories for anyone who already based work on the old commits.
assessmentCriteria: Explains that rebase rewrites commit hashes and diverges history for teammates

promptMarkdown: Why is it considered dangerous to run `git rebase` on a branch that teammates have already pulled and built commits on?

rubric.criterion: States that rebase rewrites history by creating new commits with different hashes
Explains that teammates' copies still point to the old commits, causing diverged histories, duplicate commits, or messy merge conflicts when syncing

idealAnswer: Rebasing replays commits onto a new base, which generates brand-new commit hashes. Anyone who already pulled the old commits now has a different history than the remote branch, requiring a force-push and leaving teammates with diverged branches, duplicate commits, and confusing conflicts.

answers.text: Rebasing doesn't move the old commits — it writes new ones with different SHA hashes. Teammates who already pulled the old history now have a diverged branch, so after you force-push they hit messy conflicts or end up re-merging duplicate copies of the same commits.
Because rebase rewrites commit history and requires a force push.
Rebasing automatically deletes any uncommitted files on your teammates' laptops the next time they open Git.

The main risk of rebasing a shared branch is that Git stores branches in a centralized lock table; rebasing acquires an exclusive lock that blocks teammates from pulling until the repository administrator manually clears the reflog.

concept.title: Variation comes before selection
concept.description: Mutations arise randomly, not in response to need; selection filters existing heritable variation by differential survival and reproduction.
assessmentCriteria: Rejects purposeful adaptation during an organism's lifetime and explains selection on pre-existing random variation

promptMarkdown: A student says: "Bacteria evolve antibiotic resistance because they sense the drug and mutate to survive it." What is wrong with that explanation, and how does resistance actually spread?

rubric.criterion: Clarifies that mutations occur randomly (already present by chance), not purposefully in response to the antibiotic
Explains that the antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria while the pre-existing resistant ones survive and reproduce, increasing their share of the population

idealAnswer: Bacteria do not mutate on purpose to beat a drug. Random mutations are already happening in a large population, so a few cells happen to carry traits that survive the antibiotic. The drug kills the susceptible majority, leaving the resistant cells to multiply and take over the population.

answers.text: They don't choose to mutate when they meet the drug. Random mutations already exist in a few bacteria beforehand; the antibiotic wipes out the non-resistant ones, so the lucky resistant cells survive, divide, and become most of the population.
bacteria cant mutate on purpose. random mutations hapen anyway so a few already resist the drug. antibiotic kills the rest, resistant ones survive and multiply

answers.kind: misses why the student's claim is wrong
answers.text: The resistant bacteria survive the antibiotic and reproduce so the population becomes resistant.
Each bacterium gets exposed to a small dose of antibiotic, builds up immunity during its life, and passes that learned immunity to its offspring.
